clinicalPearls: A useful distinction is drawn between true uraemic pericarditis, occurring in advanced untreated or under-dialysed renal failure before dialysis initiation, and dialysis-associated pericarditis, arising in established dialysis patients often due to inadequate dialysis or intercurrent illness.
Uraemic pericarditis correlates broadly with the degree of azotaemia, though no single threshold of urea or creatinine reliably predicts it.

A characteristic feature is that the friction rub and clinical picture often persist despite the absence of the typical diffuse ECG changes of acute pericarditis, because the inflammation spares the underlying epicardial myocardium.
The friction rub may be loud and persistent, and effusions are frequently large and haemorrhagic owing to uraemic platelet dysfunction.
Because ECG changes are typically absent, new widespread ST elevation in a uraemic patient should prompt consideration of an alternative or additional diagnosis such as myocardial injury.

The mainstay of treatment for true uraemic pericarditis is initiation or intensification of dialysis, which resolves most cases; heparin-free or minimal-heparin dialysis is preferred to reduce haemorrhagic effusion risk.

Persistent or recurrent effusion despite intensive dialysis, or the development of tamponade, may require pericardiocentesis or a pericardial window; anti-inflammatory agents have a more limited and adjunctive role.
Progression to cardiac tamponade is an important and potentially fatal complication requiring urgent recognition and drainage.
reference.pathophysiology: The pericardial inflammation of renal failure is driven by the retention of uraemic toxins and metabolic derangements accompanying severely reduced glomerular filtration, although the precise causative solutes are not fully defined. The visceral and parietal pericardial surfaces develop a fibrinous, sometimes haemorrhagic, exudative reaction. A distinctive feature is that the inflammatory process typically remains confined to the pericardium and does not extend into the subepicardial myocardium, which explains the frequent absence of the diffuse ST-segment and PR-segment changes seen in other forms of acute pericarditis. Uraemia-associated platelet dysfunction and the anticoagulation used during haemodialysis predispose to haemorrhagic effusions, which may accumulate to produce tamponade. In dialysis-associated disease, inadequate solute clearance, volume overload, intercurrent infection or inflammation are contributory.
additionalDifferentials: myocardial infarction or acute coronary syndrome
systemic lupus erythematosus or other connective tissue disease serositis
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG (typically lacks diffuse ST/PR changes; assess for ischaemia)
serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes with assessment of dialysis adequacy
full blood count and inflammatory markers
pericardial fluid analysis if drained (haemorrhagic exudate; exclude infection and malignancy)
troponin (to help distinguish concurrent myocardial injury)
redFlags: hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus indicating tamponade
large or rapidly enlarging haemorrhagic effusion
widespread ST elevation suggesting concomitant myocardial injury rather than isolated uraemic pericarditis
haemodynamic deterioration during or shortly after heparinised dialysis
fever and features suggesting superimposed purulent pericarditis
reference.prognosis: With timely initiation or intensification of dialysis most cases of true uraemic pericarditis resolve, and the outlook is generally favourable; however, large haemorrhagic effusions, tamponade and progression to constriction are recognised complications, and dialysis-associated pericarditis that responds poorly to intensified dialysis carries a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Expecting the diffuse ECG changes of typical acute pericarditis, whose absence may lead to the diagnosis being missed.
Continuing standard heparinised haemodialysis and thereby worsening a haemorrhagic effusion or precipitating tamponade.
Attributing all chest pain in a uraemic patient to pericarditis and overlooking concurrent myocardial ischaemia.
Relying on non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which are often ineffective and nephrotoxic, instead of optimising dialysis.
Under-recognising tamponade because hypotension is ascribed to intradialytic fluid shifts.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases
management: Initiate or intensify renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis), the definitive treatment that resolves most cases of true uraemic pericarditis
Use heparin-free or minimal-heparin dialysis to reduce the risk of provoking a haemorrhagic pericardial effusion given uraemic platelet dysfunction
Provide symptomatic relief for pleuritic pain, recognising that NSAIDs and colchicine are of limited benefit and NSAIDs are best avoided in advanced renal failure
Monitor with serial transthoracic echocardiography for enlarging effusion and early tamponade physiology
Perform urgent pericardiocentesis for cardiac tamponade or a large symptomatic effusion
Consider a pericardial window or pericardiectomy for recurrent, loculated, or constrictive disease unresponsive to dialysis
Co-manage with nephrology and cardiology, optimising dialysis adequacy and reviewing intercurrent illness in dialysis-associated cases
